summary: Describes Time Division Multiplexing over IP (TDMoIP), a structure-aware method of carrying TDM signals over pseudowires. Being structure-aware helps it cope better with network problems, and it allows tricks like concealing packet loss. This is an informational memo.

eli5.summary: Old-style phone circuits are chopped into packets and sent over the internet and then put back together. Knowing the structure means a lost packet is less noticeable.

questions: how to carry tdm over ip
subtitle: Transporting old-style phone circuits over modern packet networks while preserving timing and structure.

tldr.problem: Traditional phone networks use Time Division Multiplexing (TDM) to send many calls over one circuit. Modern networks use packets instead. Existing TDM equipment and services must continue working while packets travel over the internet.
tldr.mechanism: TDMoIP is a structure-aware method for carrying TDM signals inside packet pseudowires. Unlike simpler structure-agnostic approaches, TDMoIP preserves information about TDM frames and channels, enabling it to detect and conceal packet loss, recover timing, and adapt bandwidth when channels are inactive.
tldr.outcome: Phone services and other TDM applications can be transported over packet networks with quality comparable to native TDM, improving reliability during network problems and enabling new capabilities like per-channel bandwidth conservation.

facts.label: E1 frame size
facts.value: 256 bits (32 bytes total, 1 byte overhead, 31 bytes data)

today: RFC 5087 is Informational. TDMoIP remains in use in carrier networks and enterprise deployments where TDM circuit emulation over IP is required, particularly in MPLS and L2TPv3 environments. The RFC complements RFC 5086 (structure-locking approach) and other related standards. It has not been obsoleted and continues to define one of the primary methods for structure-aware TDM over pseudowires.

sections.title: Emulating TDM Circuits over Packet Networks
sections.content:
Telephony networks have long relied on Time Division Multiplexing, where many separate phone calls share one physical link by dividing it into recurring time slots. A T1 circuit, common in North America, sends 24 voice channels, each occupying one 8-bit time slot in a repeating frame that arrives 8,000 times per second.

As IP networks became prevalent, the need arose to continue operating TDM services while transporting them over packet infrastructure. The PWE3 (Pseudowire Emulation Edge-to-Edge) architecture provides mechanisms for circuit emulation over packets. TDMoIP is a specific implementation that transports TDM in packet pseudowires.

The RFC notes that despite its name, TDMoIP can operate over multiple types of packet networks: UDP over IPv4 or IPv6, MPLS, Layer 2 Tunneling Protocol version 3 (L2TPv3), and even pure Ethernet.
sections.eli5: Old phone circuit boards divide one connection into 24 separate calls. Internet packets arrive jumbled and at random times. Emulation means putting it back the way it was.

sections.title: Structure-Aware Versus Structure-Agnostic Transport
sections.content:
Two fundamentally different approaches exist for carrying TDM over packets. Structure-agnostic TDM over Packet (SAToP) treats the TDM bit-stream as an arbitrary sequence of bits and ignores any structure such as frame boundaries. This works well for unstructured TDM and over extremely reliable networks with negligible packet loss.

Structure-aware transport, like TDMoIP, explicitly preserves or represents the TDM frame structure in the packet payload. This awareness enables three advantages. First, it maintains TDM synchronization and frame alignment even when packets are lost, preventing downstream equipment from seeing spurious frames. Second, individual channels in multiplexed TDM become visible, allowing sophisticated per-channel packet loss concealment instead of just playing silence. Third, TDM signaling becomes accessible, permitting mechanisms that read, modify, or exploit signaling information.

The RFC describes three methods to ensure TDM structure integrity during transport: structure-locking (each packet contains whole frames), structure-indication (pointers show where frames begin), and structure-reassembly (individual channels are extracted and reassembled). TDMoIP implements the latter two.
sections.eli5: Structure-agnostic just ships raw bits. Structure-aware remembers how the circuit was divided, so when a packet is lost, the receiver can guess what the lost call sample probably sounded like instead of producing an ugly pop.

sections.title: Packet Format and Control
sections.content:
Every TDMoIP packet contains a 32-bit control word carrying flags and a 16-bit sequence number. The control word includes a local failure (L) flag that the sender sets when it detects problems on the TDM side (loss of signal, frame misalignment, or Alarm Indication Signal). A remote failure (R) flag indicates that the receiver is not getting TDM data, signaling failure in the reverse direction.

The payload consists of one or more PDUs (Protocol Data Units) using either AAL1 format (for constant-rate circuits), AAL2 format (for variable-rate channels), or HDLC format (for common channel signaling like SS7). An optional RTP header may precede the control word to carry explicit timing information when IWFs (interworking functions) lack a common clock.

Different packet networks require different outer headers: UDP/IP carries the IP and UDP headers, MPLS uses label stacks, L2TPv3 uses session identifiers, and pure Ethernet uses VLAN tags and a pseudo-MPLS label. The control word and payload are consistent across all transports.
sections.eli5: Each packet is labeled with status flags (local problem, remote problem) and a sequence number so the receiver knows the packet's place in the stream and whether something is missing or broken.

sections.title: AAL1 and AAL2 Adaptation
sections.content:
AAL (ATM Adaptation Layer) technologies from ATM networks are reused for TDMoIP. AAL1 provides constant-rate adaptation suitable for unchannelized TDM, structured but unchannelized TDM, or channelized TDM where all channels are always active. Each 48-byte AAL1 PDU embeds a pointer indicating where the next TDM frame begins, enabling the receiver to maintain frame synchronization even if packets arrive out of order or are lost. Multiple AAL1 PDUs may be packed into one packet.

AAL2 provides variable-rate adaptation for channelized TDM where channels are often inactive. In AAL2 mode, only active channels are sent, conserving bandwidth. Each AAL2 PDU contains 3 bytes of overhead and 1 to 64 bytes of payload. This mode is preferred when channels have variable usage (for example, when voice activity detection is employed to identify and omit silent periods) or when dynamic channel allocation is desired.

A third mode, HDLC format, is optimized for transporting common channel signaling (CCS) such as SS7, which is essential for establishing phone calls but occupies only one channel of a TDM circuit.
sections.eli5: AAL1 is best when all channels always have data. AAL2 saves bandwidth when channels are quiet. HDLC is special for the single signaling channel that orders phone calls.

sections.title: Jitter, Timing, and Packet Loss Handling
sections.content:
Packet networks introduce packet delay variation (jitter), requiring a jitter buffer at the receiver to collect packets arriving at irregular intervals and release data at a steady rate. The buffer is typically kept approximately half full, balancing the risks of overflow and underflow.

TDM networks rely on synchronous timing: every element has a clock derived from a central reference. IP networks have no such synchronization. The RFC describes four timing recovery methods. Two provide external timing (from a global source or to the IWF hardware). A third method, when a common clock is available, encodes the source clock relationship in RTP timestamps or AAL1 synchronous residual timestamp bits. The fourth, adaptive clock recovery, infers timing from observable packet arrival times using frequency or phase locked loops.

Lost packets are detected via sequence numbers. When loss is detected, the IWF outputs filler data (usually a preconfigured constant or AIS, Alarm Indication Signal) to maintain TDM timing. For voice, loss concealment algorithms attempt to estimate missing samples and minimize perceptual artifacts. Structure-aware transport enables per-channel concealment, reducing the impact of losses.
sections.eli5: Jitter buffering smooths out lumpy packet arrivals. For timing, the receiver can use an external clock, encode the sender's clock in packets, or guess from when packets arrived. Losses are filled with silence or guessed audio.

sections.title: Deployment, Security, and Limitations
sections.content:
TDMoIP SHOULD be carried over traffic-engineered networks that provide bandwidth reservation or forwarding prioritization, such as MPLS with traffic engineering or Diffserv domains with Expedited Forwarding. For best-effort networks, packet loss monitoring is essential; if congestion is detected and bandwidth cannot be reduced, the pseudowire should shut down temporarily.

Security considerations resemble those of other pseudowires. IP-based TDMoIP may use IPsec for confidentiality and authentication. L2TPv3-based TDMoIP is subject to the security considerations of RFC 3931, including the use of cookies to protect against off-path insertion attacks. Random initialization of sequence numbers and unpredictable selection of PW labels deter known-plaintext attacks and session hijacking.

The RFC acknowledges that TDMoIP emulation is imperfect: end-to-end delay may exceed native TDM, timing performance depends on PSN characteristics when using adaptive recovery, and when structure overhead is not transported, non-FAS (Frame Alignment Signal) data in that overhead is lost. However, when properly deployed with packet loss concealment, the impact on voice calls is substantially reduced compared to structure-agnostic methods.
sections.eli5: Use high-priority networks when possible. Protect with encryption if needed. Accept that delays and quality will not be exactly like TDM, but structure-aware handling makes it good enough for voice.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Set to zero (except for MPLS PSNs must be zero to avoid IP packet aliasing).

fields.name: Local Failure
fields.desc: Set when IWF detects loss of signal, frame sync, or AIS on the TDM side.

fields.name: Remote Failure
fields.desc: Set when IWF detects failure in the reverse direction (RDI).

fields.name: Defect Modifier
fields.desc: When L flag is set, qualifies the type of defect (conditioning, idle, recoverable).

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Total packet length when less than 64 bytes, zero otherwise.

fields.name: Sequence Number
fields.desc: Detects lost and misordered packets, modulo 2^16.
